To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) periadolescents are less active overall than adult rats in the locomotor test; 2) adult rats are more sensitive to acute locomotor stimulant effects of cocaine; 3) both age groups show sensitization of locomotion after repeated cocaine administration; 4) both age groups acquire i.v. cocaine self-administration with similar rapidity; 5) there is no age-related difference in nucleus accumbens dopaminergic activity under basal or cocaine-stimulation conditions
(1) periadolescent and adult rats exhibit similar behavioral and neurochemical responses to cocaine, (2) the behavioral effects of cocaine are not mediated via dopamine in the nucleus...

(1) Periadolescent rats were less active than adult rats after acute cocaine administration; (2) adult, but not periadolescent rats, demonstrated locomotor sensitization to repeated cocaine; (3) both age groups acquired cocaine self-administration similarly, but adult rats self-administered more cocaine; (4) cocaine increased nucleus accumbens extracellular dopamine similarly in periadolescents and adults; and (5) locomotor responses to cocaine were not mediated by dopamine

the behavioral and neurochemical responses to cocaine in periadolescnet vs adult animals, and we have found that the behavioral response to cocaine in the periadolescent period is different than in adults.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the behavioral effects of cocaine are not age-specific in the sense that they do not differ in the two age groups studied, but rather are age-dependent, i.e., the same effect of cocaine may occur at a different age.
periadolescents are not necessarily more sensitive to cocaine than adults.
periadolescent and adult rats do not differ in behavioral responses to cocaine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the behavioral responses to cocaine are more sensitive to the effects of development than are the neurochemical responses.
the behavioral and neurochemical responses to cocaine are similar in adolescent and adult male rats.
there are some similarities in cocaine responses across age groups, but also some differences that could be important to consider in future studies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the motor effects of cocaine may be dissociable from the reinforcing effects of the drug in the periadolescent period.
the behavioral responses to cocaine are developmentally regulated, but not in the way that was expected.
there is no single “adolescent brain,” rather there are multiple systems that develop and mature at different rates.
